card.thesis: A 200-day moving average is a slow proxy for whether the marginal buyer still controls the tape. Structural forced sellers -- pensions and mandate-bound funds de-risking after a sustained decline, and levered holders forced out by drawdown -- keep supplying stock into a market that has been falling for months, which is exactly what 'price below its own 200-day average' detects; staying out during that condition avoids selling into their hands and re-enters only once buyers have re-established control on a monthly-to-quarterly timescale. Applying the same filter independently across four largely uncorrelated exposures (US equities SPY, international developed equities EFA, long Treasuries TLT, gold GLD) means one asset's trend break does not force the whole book to cash: in a rate-driven equity bear, the flight-to-quality bid that keeps bonds and gold trending up is a countercyclical buyer the strategy rides while equities are excluded, so exposure and return both keep coming from somewhere. Pre-registered failure regime: a sideways, choppy, low-trend market has no edge for this filter and pays repeated whipsaw entries/stop-outs against a benchmark that simply sits still; and a regime where every asset class de-rates together (a simultaneous equity-and-bond bear, e.g. a rate shock) removes nearly the whole book to cash-like exposure at once, leaving the strategy flat while a buy-and-hold benchmark may partially recover before the filter re-engages.
